newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM to discuss tensions in northwest.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM to discuss tensions in northwest.

text.p: Cambodian co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh will discuss a tense standoff that erupted in Battambang at the weekend with top officials here, Battambang's deputy governor Serey Kosal said on Wednesday.

Serey Kosal, who flew into the northern town of Siem Reap with a large delegation of military and police officials loyal to his royalist FUNCINPEC party, said he had come to discuss with Ranariddh recent problems with the ex-communist Cambodian People's Party (CPP).
"We are studying the situation very carefully and seriously because we know very well the tactics of communists," he said. "If we retreat, communists profit and make problems again."

On Friday, a FUNCINPEC soldier shot a CPP military policeman in the leg during an argument at a private home in Battambang, Cambodia's second largest city, located about 300 km (188 miles) northwest of Phnom Penh.

The dispute escalated into a row between the two political parties that make up Cambodia's coalition government when Serey Kosal called in 5,000 FUNCINPEC troops to the area and the CPP put its forces on alert.
The coalition government has been shaken by deep differences over issues ranging from power-sharing to control over defecting Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
Tensions were exacerbated last week when the brother-in-law of second prime minister Hun Sen -- a member of the CPP -- was gunned down by an unidentified man outside a Phnom Penh restaurant.

Serey Kosal said he had called his troops back at the request of armed forces deputy chief of staff Lieutenant General Nhiek Bun Chhay of FUNCINPEC, who was also due to attend the meeting with Ranariddh.
He warned, however, that he would not tolerate alleged intimidation by CPP troops ahead of national elections in 1998.
"We do not accept trouble from the CPP. We won't accept it from now until the elections," he said.
Analysts said tensions are likely to continue through the 1998 general elections, which will pit the coalition partners against each other.
